name: Federalism
summary: Federalism is the theory and advocacy of dividing final authority between member units and common institutions, usually in an entrenched constitution that neither level can alter alone. Its founding arguments hold that this double division, together with checks inside each government and an extended union of many interests, restrains rulers and majorities, lets diverse communities govern themselves, and secures defence and commerce at the centre. It is a structural doctrine and speaks to few questions outside the form and limits of government.
scope: Constitutional federalism as the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy defines it (a territorial division of power between member units and a common government, including coming-together and holding-together federations), as set out in the texts it names: the Federalist papers of Madison, Hamilton and Jay, Montesquieu on the confederate republic, Althusius, and Mill on federal representative governments. It excludes the US Federalist Party, the states-rights politics of nullification, Proudhon's anarchist federalism and the later European federalist movement except as the Stanford entry reports them, and it answers a statement only where these texts take a position on it.

missingStatements.text: A federal government should make laws that apply directly to individual citizens.
missingStatements.rationale: Federalist No. 16 and Mill both hold that a union acting only through its member governments is a mere alliance, and that an effective federal government must reach individual citizens itself.

quotes.text: It must carry its agency to the persons of the citizens.
A union between the governments only is a mere alliance, and subject to all the contingencies which render alliances precarious.

notes: Later pass under rules 7. The earlier pass answered about 130 statements on the strength of a Wikipedia summary and the remark that adherents differ; those answers were nulled or replaced here, because a structural doctrine that is silent on a statement gives no position (AUDIT_RULES.md section 3). Themes searched: the division of powers and its guard (Stanford entry, Britannica, Federalist Nos. 9, 10, 16, 22, 28, 33, 39, 45, 46, 51, 62, Mill ch. 17, Montesquieu Book 9), majority rule and minority protection, second chambers and indirect election, secession, resistance to usurpation, subsidiarity, minority accommodation, property, defence and commerce. The Federalist essays are used only where they argue about the federal union or the checks that make it work; their republican and presidential claims are not federalism's own and are left out.
